q: Does the block-diagonal (or fully diagonal) approximation of the Fubini-Study metric preserve the QNG iteration-count advantage as ansatz depth grows, and at what depth does the approximation break down?
basis: This replication only tested a single-layer 4-parameter HEA. PennyLane's approx='block-diag' was adequate here and matched full-metric behavior to machine precision, but the paper hand-derives the full analytic F for exactly this shallow case. Deeper HEAs / brick-wall ansatze have entangling structure that fills in off-block-diagonal QFI elements, and it is unclear at what depth diagonal/block-diagonal QNG stops matching full-metric QNG.
next_steps: Run a depth sweep (1, 2, 4, 8 layers) of a brick-wall HEA on the same H2 Hamiltonian and on a 4-6 qubit LiH toy, comparing three optimizers: (i) vanilla GD, (ii) block-diagonal QNG, (iii) full-metric QNG using qml.QNGOptimizer(approx=None). Measure iteration count to chemical accuracy AND total quantum-expectation-evaluation count. Report the depth at which block-diagonal QNG loses >20% of the iteration-count advantage that full QNG retains.

q: How does the QNG iteration-count advantage over vanilla GD change when finite shot noise and parameter-shift gradient evaluation replace exact statevector expectations?
basis: This replication used a statevector simulator with exact expectations, matching the paper's 'no approximation' setup. Real hardware and NISQ-realistic simulation require finite shots, which inject stochastic noise into both the gradient and the metric-tensor estimate. QNG's F^{-1} step is known to be sensitive to metric-tensor noise (small eigenvalues get amplified). Whether the 1.45-1.75x speedup survives realistic shot budgets is an open, practical question.
next_steps: Repeat the exact H2 experiment on default.qubit but with finite shots per expectation (shots=100, 1k, 10k, 100k). Use parameter-shift gradients and a Hadamard-test-based metric-tensor with the same shot budget. Measure (a) iteration count to reach |E-E_exact|<1e-2, (b) variance of the trajectory across 20 seeds, (c) rate of F-inversion blowup requiring the lambda regulariser. Compare against vanilla GD with the same total shot budget re-allocated to gradient estimation only. Speedup should be measured in total shots, not iterations.

q: Does QNG deliver similar iteration-count speedups on QAOA and quantum-machine-learning (variational classifier) loss landscapes, or is the advantage specific to VQE-style eigenvalue objectives?
basis: The paper and this replication address VQE only. QAOA has a highly non-convex energy landscape with p-dependent parameter concentration; QML classifier losses can have plateaus and barren-plateau behavior that differ from VQE eigenvalue landscapes. The geometric-preconditioning argument for QNG is loss-agnostic, so in principle it should help, but the empirical picture is unclear.
next_steps: Set up (i) QAOA on max-cut for a random 6-vertex 3-regular graph, p=1,2,4; (ii) a variational classifier on a 4-qubit encoding of the iris dataset. For each, run vanilla GD, Adam, and QNG at matched hyperparameters. Measure iteration count to reach 95% of the best achievable loss, over 10 seeds. If QNG's advantage evaporates on QAOA, characterize the loss-landscape features (barren-plateau proximity, F condition number) that predict this.

q: How robust is QNG to realistic hardware noise (depolarizing, amplitude/phase damping, coherent overrotation), and does the F-inversion step amplify noise-induced errors more than vanilla-GD does?
basis: The paper studies noise-free simulation. On NISQ hardware, both the energy expectation and the metric-tensor entries are biased by decoherence and coherent errors. QNG's F^{-1} preconditioning could either compensate for a systematic overrotation (favorable) or amplify a biased metric estimate into a wildly-wrong step direction (unfavorable). No quantitative characterization exists in this replication.
next_steps: Re-run the H2 Fig. 5 experiment under three PennyLane noise models: (i) depolarizing at p=1e-3, 1e-2, 1e-1 per 2-qubit gate; (ii) amplitude-damping at T1=50us with 100ns gate time; (iii) coherent overrotation of 1%, 5% on all Ry gates. For each, compare vanilla GD vs QNG convergence to a shifted noisy-ground-state fixed point. Report: (a) whether QNG still beats GD in iterations, (b) whether the noisy-fixed-point offset from true ground state is worse under QNG (due to F-inversion bias), and (c) how lambda regularisation on F trades off F-inversion stability against optimization speed.

q: Can QNG be productively combined with adaptive-momentum optimizers (Adam-QNG, RMSProp-QNG), and does such a hybrid outperform pure QNG on shallow VQE problems where both individual optimizers already converge fast?
basis: The paper uses fixed-learning-rate SGD-style updates for both baselines. Modern classical optimization overwhelmingly uses adaptive methods (Adam, RMSProp, LAMB). A natural-gradient step with an Adam-style second-moment learning-rate schedule --- effectively rescaling F^{-1} grad by running variance --- is a straightforward hybrid that has been proposed for classical ML (K-FAC + Adam) but is not yet standard in quantum optimization. Whether the F^{-1} preconditioning and the diagonal variance rescaling are redundant, complementary, or antagonistic on VQE landscapes is unknown.
next_steps: Implement Adam-QNG as: m = beta1*m + (1-beta1)*grad; v = beta2*v + (1-beta2)*grad^2; theta -= eta * F^{-1} * m / (sqrt(v)+eps). Compare Adam-QNG, pure QNG, pure Adam, and vanilla GD on (i) H2 Fig. 5 replication with tight tolerance 1e-6, (ii) 4-qubit LiH VQE, (iii) 6-qubit BeH2 VQE. Metric: iteration count and expectation-evaluation count to reach chemical accuracy. Prediction to falsify: 'the diagonal Adam variance rescaling and the F^{-1} off-diagonal correlation preconditioning capture different curvature information and combine additively for a >1.5x further speedup over the max of either alone.'
